retrieved_evidence.title: APOE and Alzheimer's disease: advances in genetics, pathophysiology, and therapeutic approaches.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The APOE ε4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease and the APOE ε2 allele the strongest genetic protective factor after multiple large scale genome-wide association studies and genome-wide association meta-analyses. However, no therapies directed at APOE are currently available. Although initial studies causally linked APOE with amyloid-β peptide aggregation and clearance, over the past 5 years our understanding of APOE pathogenesis has expanded beyond amyloid-β peptide-centric mechanisms to tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.title: ApoE in Alzheimer's disease: pathophysiology and therapeutic strategies.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

state.research_summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), and evidence indicates it is present in more than half of all AD cases. Multiple large-scale genetic studies confirm that APOE ε4 significantly increases AD risk, while the ε2 allele is protective [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. A key finding from recent research is that APOE ε4 impacts over half of all AD cases, underscoring its central role in the disease's genetic architecture [pubmed_36348357]. Although APOE ε4 is strongly associated with AD, not all carriers develop the disease, and some individuals with the protective ε2 allele do develop AD, indicating the influence of additional genetic and environmental factors [pubmed_33576571]. The pathophysiological mechanisms of APOE extend beyond amyloid-β aggregation to include tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485]. Thus, while APOE ε4 is present in more than half of Alzheimer's patients, its presence alone is neither necessary nor sufficient for disease development.
